# Deuteronomy 24 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Verses 1–4: Divorce and Remarriage

**Overview.** All commentators agree these four verses form a single "case law" sentence (the protasis in vv. 1–3, the apodosis in v. 4). The passage does not *institute* divorce but *regulates* an existing practice, and its main point is the prohibition of a first husband remarrying his divorced wife after she has been married to another.

### v. 1

- **"Some indecency" (Hebrew *ervat davar*, lit. "nakedness of a thing"):** The Hebrew term refers to something sexually improper — not proven adultery (which carried the death penalty, Lev 20:10) and not mere trivial dislike. The phrase generally refers to sexual indecency such as indecent exposure or some form of sexual misconduct short of capital adultery. [(Precept Austin)](https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-24-commentary)

- **Rabbinic debate:** The school of Shammai restricted this to sexual immorality; the school of Hillel allowed divorce for anything displeasing, even burning a meal. Jesus (Matthew 19:3–9) sided with the stricter interpretation, defining "uncleanness" as *porneia* (sexual immorality). [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm) [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **The certificate of divorce:** A written legal document (*sepher kerithuth*, "book of cutting off") was required — divorce could not be done by mere oral declaration. This provided a cooling-off period, protected the woman from arbitrary dismissal, and gave her legal proof she was free to remarry. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/) [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- **Concession, not command:** Both older and newer commentators stress this. Ellicott calls it "a distinct concession to the weakness of Israel — not the ideal standard of the Law." Jesus confirmed this: "Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so" (Matt 19:8). [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm) [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **Why the text speaks only of the husband divorcing:** Guzik notes the Law gives "case law" principles — the same principle applies reciprocally to a wife. Jesus in Mark 10:12 applied the principle to a wife divorcing her husband. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** adds that "uncleanness" (*ervah*) could include a variety of serious offences but excludes trivial matters. Divorce for adultery was not in view because adultery was a capital crime. [(Garner-Howes, StudyLight)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-24.html)

### v. 2

- **The divorced woman was free to remarry.** The text neither commands nor prohibits remarriage, but assumes it as permissible. In that society, a single woman had few options besides remarriage or returning to her father's house. [(Precept Austin)](https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-24-commentary)

- Rashi (Jewish commentator, cited by Ellicott) remarks that "the Scripture intimates that the end of such a marriage will be that he will hate her." [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm)

### v. 3

- The second husband may either divorce her (under the same regulations) or die. Either way, she is released from the second marriage. [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm)

### v. 4

- **"Her former husband … may not take her again":** This is the main point of the entire case-law unit. The prohibition prevents casual or "revolving-door" marriages. It made divorce a weighty, irreversible decision. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/) [(Precept Austin)](https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-24-commentary)

- **Why is she "defiled"?** Gill explains it is not moral defilement by adultery (she may lawfully marry another man after the second husband dies), but defilement *with respect to her first husband* — she is now alienated and prohibited to him. The prohibition protected the sanctity of the second marriage and prevented wife-swapping. [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm) [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **"An abomination before the LORD":** This strong language shows God takes the permanence of marriage seriously. Thompson (cited by Guzik) notes the idea that unchastity defiles the land appears also in Leviticus 18:25, 28; Jeremiah 3:2, 9; Hosea 4:3. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **The ESV Study Bible note** (via Precept Austin) offers an alternative reading: the law may protect the woman from financial exploitation. By divorcing her, the first husband acquired her dowry; if she remarried, she received a second dowry. The first husband is forbidden to remarry her simply to acquire her second dowry. [(Precept Austin)](https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-24-commentary)

- **Jeremiah 3:1 connection:** Ellicott notes that Jeremiah 3:1 uses this law as a stunning picture of God's grace: "They say, If a man put away his wife … shall he return unto her again? … But thou hast played the harlot with many lovers; yet return again to me, saith the LORD." God does for Israel what the Law forbids a human husband to do. [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm)

---

#### Where Protestant Traditions Differ on vv. 1–4

**Reformed / John Piper (Desiring God):** Piper argues from Deuteronomy 24:4 that the "one-flesh" relationship is *not obliterated* even by divorce and remarriage — hence the woman is "defiled" by remarriage (v. 4). He sees this as Old Testament evidence that remarriage after divorce is illegitimate while both spouses are alive. He concludes all remarriage after divorce is prohibited except when a spouse has died. However, he also says a second marriage, once entered, should not be broken up — promises should be kept and the union consecrated to God through repentance. [(Desiring God)](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/divorce-and-remarriage-a-position-paper)

**Reformed / R.C. Sproul (Ligonier):** Sproul takes the more common Protestant position that Jesus allows divorce and remarriage in cases of *porneia* (sexual immorality) and Paul adds desertion by an unbeliever (1 Cor 7:15). The Deuteronomy 24 law was a concession to fallen human beings, not God's ideal. He notes the rabbinic dispute between Shammai and Hillel over what constitutes the "uncleanness," with Jesus taking the stricter Shammai interpretation. [(Ligonier)](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/divorce-and-remarriage)

**Pentecostal / Calvary Chapel (David Guzik, Enduring Word):** Guzik holds that Jesus interpreted "uncleanness" as sexual immorality broadly construed (not just adultery). Divorce is permitted but never commanded; the offended spouse may choose to forgive. Biblical grounds include sexual immorality (Matt 19:9) and abandonment by an unbelieving spouse (1 Cor 7:15). Guzik also argues the principle applies reciprocally to wives. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** The commentary notes the text does not sanction divorce but regulates it. Adultery is not in view (it was a capital crime). The Hillel-Shammai debate is noted, with Shammai's stricter interpretation closer to Jesus' meaning. The text makes no provision for a wife initiating divorce, though later Jewish law did allow it in limited circumstances. [(Garner-Howes, StudyLight)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-24.html)

**Older Anglican (Ellicott):** Stresses that divorce is a concession, not the ideal. "Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, suffered you" is the divine comment. The law actually enforced fell short of the ideal, which "has never varied." Ellicott also beautifully notes Jeremiah 3:1's use of this law to illustrate God's scandalous grace. [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm)

> **Note:** I was unable to find dedicated verse-by-verse treatments from Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Catholic/Orthodox (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), or modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org) sites in the search results. These gaps are noted.

## v. 5: Exemption for the Newly Married

- A newly married man was exempt from military service and public business for one full year. This was an extension of the principle in Deuteronomy 20:7 (where the betrothed man could return from war). [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **"Bring joy/happiness to his wife":** The husband's duty is to cheer his wife, to make her glad. Guzik notes this is not passive — happiness comes through the husband's purposeful, Spirit-enabled leadership. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/) [(Precept Austin)](https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-24-commentary)

- **Purpose:** The law honoured marriage, allowed the couple to establish a strong foundation, begin a family, and bond before the husband faced the risks of war. It also served as a guard against divorce. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/) [(Pulpit Commentary, via BibleHub)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- Gill notes the exemption was from war, taxes, public office — anything that would take him from home. He adds that Alexander the Great, taught by Aristotle (who was taught by a Jew), sent his newly married soldiers home to winter with their wives. [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm)

---

## v. 6: Millstones as Pledge

- **"Do not take a pair of millstones or even an upper millstone":** The millstone was essential for daily bread — grinding grain into flour. Taking it as collateral deprived a family of their very sustenance. The principle: do not take a person's livelihood as security for a loan. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/) [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- Ellicott notes this is "the production of primitive and simple times, when men had little more than the bare necessaries of life to offer as security — their own clothing, or the mill-stones … being almost their only portable property." [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- The phrase "for he taketh a man's life to pledge" (KJV) means taking what his life depends on. [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm)

---

## v. 7: Kidnapping a Capital Crime

- Kidnapping an Israelite to enslave or sell him was punishable by death. The same principle is stated in Exodus 21:16. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- The death penalty was by strangling, according to Jewish tradition (Targum of Jonathan, cited by Gill). [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- Thompson (cited by Guzik) notes the offence must have been common in the ancient Near East, "to judge from other law codes which legislate against the practice." [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **"Purge the evil from among you":** Capital punishment served both to remove the offender and to deter the crime, preventing communal guilt. [(Garner-Howes, StudyLight)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-24.html)

---

## vv. 8–9: Leprosy and the Lesson of Miriam

- **"Be careful to diligently follow everything the Levitical priests instruct you":** The detailed laws for diagnosing and quarantining skin diseases are in Leviticus 13–14. The priests served as public health officials as well as spiritual leaders. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **Miriam as a warning:** God struck Miriam with leprosy for rebelling against Moses (Numbers 12). She was confined outside the camp for seven days despite being a prophetess and Moses' sister. The point (per Ellicott) is that if someone as prominent as Miriam was not exempt, no one should expect exemption. "There might be a tendency to relax the law in the case of great or wealthy persons." [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- Gill adds that the Miriam example also warns against "entertaining evil suspicions, and surmises of persons in power and authority, and speaking evil of them." [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- The Hebrew term *ṣara'at* covers a range of skin diseases and is also applied to mould in clothes and houses (Lev 14:55). [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

---

## vv. 10–13: Humane Lending and Pledges

### vv. 10–11

- **"Do not enter his house to collect security":** The lender must wait outside; the borrower chooses and brings out the pledge. This preserved the poor man's dignity and prevented the lender from seizing essential items. Meyer (cited by Guzik): "What courtesy and respect for the feelings of another prompted this injunction!" [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- Gill cites the Jewish canon that a pledge could not be taken without the knowledge and permission of the Sanhedrin (court). [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm)

### vv. 12–13

- If the borrower was poor and gave his cloak (often the only portable property), the lender had to return it by sunset so the man could sleep in it. This meant the lender might have to fetch and return the pledge daily — making the pledge more trouble than it was worth, thus encouraging outright generosity. [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm) [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **"It shall be righteousness to you before the LORD":** The LXX translates this as "alms" or "mercy." It is not justifying righteousness but a concrete act of covenant faithfulness that God approves — much like Matthew 6:1 where "alms" is called "righteousness." [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm) [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- **"He … will bless you":** The poor man's grateful prayer would invoke God's blessing on the merciful lender. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

---

## vv. 14–15: Pay the Hired Worker Promptly

- The command repeats and expands Leviticus 19:13 ("the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning"). [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- **"Poor and needy … whether a brother or a foreigner":** The protection extends equally to Israelites and resident aliens. The day labourer lived hand-to-mouth and depended on each day's wage to feed his family. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/) [(Gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- **"He may cry out to the LORD against you":** James 5:4 echoes this: "the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts." God Himself hears and avenges the oppressed worker. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- Merrill (cited by Guzik): the hireling's low status "was no excuse to deny him his rights. In fact, he enjoyed such status with God that he could and might cry out to the Lord against the stingy, dishonest employer." [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

---

## v. 16: Personal Responsibility for Sin

- **"Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers":** Each person bears the penalty for his own sin. This principle of individual responsibility is later expounded in detail in Ezekiel 18. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/) [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- **Apparent exceptions (Achan, Joshua 7):** When a whole family was punished, it suggests family complicity in the crime. Amaziah son of Joash is noted in 2 Kings 14:6 and 2 Chronicles 25:4 as having observed this law — he executed the murderers of his father but not their children. [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm) [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- Ellicott contrasts this with Persian practice: Daniel's accusers' families were thrown to the lions with them (Daniel 6:24), showing Israel's law was uniquely just. [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- Kalland (cited by Guzik): "Though shame and other consequences of crime fall naturally on one's family … the punishment to be exacted for a crime falls on the perpetrator alone." [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

---

## vv. 17–18: Justice for the Vulnerable

- **Three categories recur:** the foreigner (stranger/alien), the fatherless (orphan), and the widow — those with no social advocate in the ancient world. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **"Do not deny justice"** — the courts must not be biased against those without status or wealth. **"Do not take a widow's cloak as security"** — even what was permitted for others (temporary pledge of a cloak, vv. 12–13) was forbidden for the widow, who had no husband to advocate for her. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- **"Remember that you were slaves in Egypt":** This motivation appears six times in Deuteronomy (5:15; 15:15; 16:12; 24:18; 24:22). Israel's own experience of oppression should produce compassion, not hardness. [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm) [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- Ellicott offers a Christological reading: the Lord's special care for the "stranger" throughout the Old Testament is "like a path strewn with flowers, in expectation of the coming of one that is greatly beloved" — Jesus, who came as a stranger with "no room for Him in the inn." [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm)

---

## vv. 19–22: Gleaning Rights for the Poor

### v. 19 — Forgotten Sheaf
- If a harvester forgot a sheaf in the field, he was not to return for it. It belonged to the foreigner, orphan, and widow. This is the law under which Ruth gleaned in Boaz's field (Ruth 2:2–3, 16). [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

### v. 20 — Olive Trees
- After beating olives from the trees, the farmer was not to go over the branches a second time. Remaining olives were for the poor. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

### v. 21 — Grapes
- The same principle applied to the vineyard: no second pass over the vines. Gleanings were for the vulnerable. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

### v. 22 — Remember Egypt (again)
- The refrain returns: Israel's own memory of slavery should produce generosity, not greed. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

**Key points from commentators:**
- This was God's welfare system: it commanded farmers to be generous, while preserving the dignity of the poor, who had to work actively to gather their food. Merrill: "This permitted the recipient to salvage his own honor while at the same time delivering the landowner from any sense of arrogant control." [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

- The gleaning law is connected with Pentecost in Leviticus 23:22. Ellicott beautifully notes that "never was such care for the widow and the poor manifested as after the day of Pentecost in the New Testament," when "great grace was upon them all" and "neither was there any among them that lacked" (Acts 4:33–34). [(Ellicott)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/24.htm)

- This was not the only provision for the poor; Deuteronomy 14:28–29 and 26:12–15 commanded a tithe every three years for the Levite, foreigner, orphan, and widow. [(Enduring Word)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-24/)

---

## Summary of Gaps

I was unable to locate dedicated treatments of this chapter from:
- **Methodist/Wesleyan** sources (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com)
- **Lutheran** sources (lcms.org, 1517.org)
- **Catholic** sources (newadvent.org, catholic.com)
- **Orthodox** sources (oca.org)
- **Modern scholarship** (bibleodyssey.org) — though NET Bible notes and ESV Study Bible notes were accessed via Precept Austin
- **Prosperity/Word of Faith/Hyper-grace** — no results from approved sites discussing Deuteronomy 24 through these lenses

The most notable Protestant difference found was between the **Piper/Desiring God "no remarriage while spouse lives"** position and the mainstream Protestant position (Sproul/Ligonier, Guzik/Enduring Word, Garner-Howes) allowing divorce and remarriage on grounds of sexual immorality and abandonment.
